content: The sugar-apple, also referred to as the custard-apple in some regions, is a plant species scientifically known as Annona squamosa. It is native to the tropical Americas, although its precise native range is uncertain due to widespread cultivation. It is believed to have originated in the Caribbean, with the species first described in Jamaica. This plant is a semi-evergreen shrub or small tree that typically grows to a height of 6 to 8 meters. Its leaves are alternately arranged, simple, and oblong-lanceolate in shape, measuring 5 to 17 cm in length and 2 to 5 cm in width. The flowers are approximately 5 to 3 cm across, with six petals that are yellow-green and spotted with purple at the base. The fruit of the sugar-apple is generally round or oval, resembling a small pine cone, with a diameter of 6 to 10 cm and a weight of 100 to 230 grams. Its skin is scaly or lumpy in texture. The edible flesh of the fruit is white to light yellow in color and has a custard-like texture and flavor. The seeds are dispersed throughout the fruit's flesh, are blackish-brown in color, measure 12 to 18 mm in length, and are hard and shiny. The sugar-apple is known by various names across different cultures. In English, it is commonly called sugar-apple or sweetsop, and sometimes custard-apple, although this term is technically incorrect as it usually refers to a related species. In Latin America, it is known by names such as anón, anón de azúcar, anona blanca, fruta do conde, cachiman, and saramuyo. In India, it is called aarticum, shareefa, sitaphal, or seethaphal, which translates to Sita fruit due to its resemblance to the head of Sita. In Indonesia, it is referred to as srimatikiya or more commonly srikaya. In Taiwan, it is called Sakya because one cultivar resembles the top part of the head of Sakyamuni (Buddha), and it is also known as Buddha Head. In Burmese, it is called aajaa thee. In the Philippines, it is known as atis. In Thailand, it is called Noi-Na (น้อยหน่า), which is also the colloquial term for a hand grenade due to its appearance. In Vietnam, it is referred to as trái mãng cầu ta or na. In Brazil, it is called fruta do conde, pinha, or ata. The sugar-apple is high in calories and serves as a good source of iron. It is the most widely cultivated species of the Annona genus and is grown extensively throughout tropical and warmer subtropical regions. It was introduced to southern Asia before 1590. The plant has become naturalized as far north as southern Florida in the United States and as far south as Bahia in Brazil. However, it is considered an invasive species in some areas. Like most Annona species, it thrives in tropical or subtropical climates with summer temperatures ranging from 25°C to 41°C and mean winter temperatures above 15°C. It is sensitive to cold and frost, with defoliation occurring below 10°C and death at temperatures slightly below freezing. The plant requires annual rainfall exceeding 700 mm and does not produce fruit well during droughts. Despite this, it is a prolific fruit bearer, capable of producing fruit within two to three years. A five-year-old tree can yield up to 50 fruits. In Florida, poor fruit production has been reported due to a lack of natural pollinators, as honeybees struggle to penetrate the tightly closed female flowers. However, hand pollination using a natural fiber brush has proven effective in increasing yields. In the Philippines, the fruit is a common food source for the Philippine fruit bat (kabag or kabog), which aids in seed dispersal across islands. A company in the Philippines also produces sugar-apple wine. The sugar-apple serves as a host plant for the larvae of the butterfly Graphium agamemnon (Tailed Jay). In India, the plant is used in some communities to prepare a hair tonic, and its seeds are ground and applied to eliminate lice from hair.
